title: M-L-Ch

cards: The elders of Israel walk to Ramah, to the prophet Samuel, who is old now, and put a request in front of him: "now make us a king to judge us like all the nations." Like everyone else.
A palace, a crown, someone to lead the army out. The text says plainly how Samuel took it: "But the thing displeased Samuel." He goes to pray about it, and the answer he gets cuts two ways.
That answer, and the Hebrew word for king inside it, is where today begins.

teach.b: M-L-Ch. Mem, lamed, chaf. Melech, a king.
Malchut, kingship, a kingdom. And the verb, to reign. Turn it four ways.
First, the answer Samuel gets. God tells him to listen to the people, and then: "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." Reign is this root.
A human throne is granted, but with a long warning about what kings take: sons, daughters, fields, harvests. Kingship in the Bible starts with that tension built in. Second, a song sung long before.

teach.h: THE LORD SHALL REIGN FOR EVER.
teach.b: On the far shore of the sea, after the crossing, Moses and the people sing, and the song ends: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever." They have no king of their own yet, and they sing that. Third, the blessings.

teach.h: MELECH HA-OLAM: KING OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: The standard blessing names God melech ha-olam, king of the world, so the word comes up over bread, over wine, over a new fruit. Fourth, a kingdom you accept.
The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, asks why the Shema's first paragraph comes before the next.

teach.h: THE YOKE OF THE KINGDOM, ACCEPTED.
teach.b: Its answer: so that a person first takes on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, ol malchut shamayim, and only then the yoke of the commandments.
Kingship, in that picture, isn't seized or imposed. It's accepted, by the one saying the words, morning and evening. Which leaves a plain question: who, or what, rules here?

how: Jews say the Shema morning and evening, which the Mishnah calls accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, and the standard blessing names God melech ha-olam, king of the world; on Rosh Hashanah a section of the service, Malchuyot, is devoted to God's kingship.

o: kingship: a king, a kingdom and the right to reign

games.q: you're Samuel. the elders want a king like all the nations, and it hurts. you pray. what answer comes back?
o: refuse them; Israel needs no king.
listen to them: they have rejected me, not you. but warn them.
pick the strongest man you can find.
games.why: "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me." the throne is granted, with a warning about what kings take.

practice: Look back over the last few hours and ask what's been sitting on the throne: your phone, a deadline, a worry, a grudge, someone's opinion of you.
Name it plainly without scolding yourself, then ask what you'd want ruling instead, kindness, a promise, God, your own best judgment, and let that sit on the throne for the rest of this quiet.
If you pray, you can say the Shema, the way the Mishnah describes taking on the kingdom.

wordCard.voice: M-L-Ch. Mem, lamed, chaf: melech, a king; malchut, kingship; the reign the elders asked for and the one sung at the sea. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: kingship, kingdom, reign. from melech, king.

carryVoice: Your line: kingship. Something always sits on the throne; the root asks who put it there. Rest well.
